# General mycology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Basics of infectious diseases > General mycology*

[Original Article Link](/library/KM0Upg)

---

## Summary

Fungi are widespread in the environment and many species colonize the human body without evidence of infection. Mycoses are infections caused by fungi such as <u>dermatophytes</u> (e.g., <u>Trichophyton</u>), <u>yeasts</u> (e.g., <u>Candida</u>), or <u>molds</u> (e.g., <u>Aspergillus</u>).




See also “<u>Overview of fungal infections</u>,” “<u>Candidiasis</u>,” “<u>Aspergillosis</u>,” and “<u>Dermatophyte infections</u>.”

---

## Basics of mycology

### Overview of mycological terminology [[1]](/library/bRYHlK)




* Hyphae: tubular, branching filaments of fungal cells, with or without septae

* Septa: hyphal <u>cell wall</u> divisions, typically porous

* Pseudohyphae

* A <u>hypha</u>-like filament formed by a chain of <u>budding</u> <u>yeast</u> cells that have not become detached from each other

* <u>Pseudohyphae</u> can be identified by the presence of constrictions at the site of origin.

* Mycelium: a <u>haploid</u> and multicellular network of <u>hyphae</u> forming a thread-like structure

* Pseudomycelium: <u>mycelium</u>-like mass of <u>pseudohyphae</u>

* Thallus: the vegetative body of a fungus

* Sporangia: a <u>spore-forming</u> structure

* Spores

* <u>Haploid</u>, reproductive particles that can be formed on reproductive <u>hyphae</u> or <u>mycelium</u>

* May result from asexual (e.g., sporangiospores) or sexual reproduction

* Sporangiophore: modified <u>hyphae</u> bearing sporangia

* <u>Conidia</u>

* Asexual spore of a fungus

* May bud in <u>clusters</u> of chains

* Produced by most pathogenic fungi

* Conidiophore: simple or branched <u>hyphae</u> on which <u>conidia</u> are produced

* Germ tube

* An outgrowth produced by spores during germination

* No constrictions at the site of origin

* Anamorph: asexual reproductive state of a fungus

* Teleomorph: sexual reproductive state of a fungus

* Conidium: an asexual fungal spore formed from a vegetative <u>yeast</u>, hyphal cell, or a specialized conidiogenous cell

* Microconidium: a small asexual fungal spore

* Macroconidium: a large asexual fungal spore

### Fungi structure and morphology [[2]](/library/8JcODW0)




Fungi vary widely in size and shape, from unicellular to multicellular forms. Microscopic fungi are either <u>molds</u> or <u>yeasts</u> or both.




* General characteristics of fungi

* Fungi are <u>eukaryotes</u>.

* Most are obligate or facultative aerobes.

* Can be unicellular, multicellular, or dimorphic

* Divide asexually, sexually, or both

* Fungi are chemotrophic organisms, i.e., they secrete enzymes to degrade organic substrates.

* Structure of fungi

* Fungal cell wall: composed of chitin, glucans, and mannans

* Fungal cell membrane: contains ergosterol (analogous to <u>cholesterol</u> in humans)

* <u>Cell membrane</u> component unique to fungal species

* Key enzymes in its synthetic pathway include squalene epoxidase and 14–α–demethylase, which converts lanosterol to <u>ergosterol</u>.

* Morphology of fungi

* Monomorphic fungi: fungi that exist exclusively as either <u>yeast</u> or <u>mold</u>

* <u>Yeasts</u>: unicellular fungi, occasionally organize into <u>hyphae</u> and <u>pseudohyphae</u>

* <u>Molds</u>: multicellular fungi, organized into <u>hyphae</u>

* For clinical significance and further discussion, see “<u>Yeasts</u>” and “<u>Molds</u>” below.

* Dimorphic fungi: fungi that can exist as both <u>mold</u> or <u>yeast</u>, depending on temperature

* <u>Molds</u> typically grow at approx. 20Â°C and <u>yeasts</u> grow at 37Â°C.

* Examples: <u>Histoplasma capsulatum</u>, <u>Blastomyces dermatitidis</u>, <u>Coccidioides immitis</u>, <u>Paracoccidioides brasiliensis</u>, and <u>Sporothrix schenckii</u>

* Most commonly cause subacute pulmonary infections





> [!NOTE]
> Fungi represent a kingdom separate from plants and animals. They extract energy (e.g., sugar and <u>proteins</u>) from living or dead organic matter.




> [!NOTE]
> To remember the temperatures at which the different forms of <u>dimorphic fungi</u> exist, think: <u>Mold</u> in the cold, <u>yeast</u> in the heat! <u>Dimorphic fungi</u> exist as <u>mold</u>s at cooler temperatures (cold) and as <u>yeast</u>s at warmer temperatures (heat).

## Physiology of fungi

### Fungi replication [[1]](/library/bRYHlK)[[3]](/library/NIc-1d0)[[4]](/library/KIcUdd0)




#### Overview




Fungi reproduce through sexually and/or asexually produced spores.




* Asexual reproduction

* Occurs through <u>mitotic</u> division

* Produces unicellular spores that are genetically identical to the parent body

* Sexual reproduction

* Occurs through <u>meiotic</u> division

* Produces zygospores, which result from the union of two compatible <u>nuclei</u> and are genetically different from the parent bodies

* Introduces genetic diversity





#### Asexual reproduction of fungi




* Mechanisms

* Asexual spore production (most common mode of reproduction)

* Spores may be released outside or within a special reproductive structure, where they grow independently.

* A <u>haploid cell</u> is produced via <u>mitosis</u> and released from the parent body (e.g., <u>hypha</u>, sporogenous cell)

* Fungal fragmentation: a portion of the <u>mycelium</u> splits from the body of the fungus, with the resulting fragment being capable of replication

* Binary fission: a cell undergoes nuclear division and splits into two daughter cells capable of replicating

* Budding

* An outgrowth, bud, or appendage develops on the surface of <u>the cell</u> or the <u>hypha</u>, with its <u>cytoplasm</u> being continuous with that of the parent cell.

* The <u>nucleus</u> of the parent cell divides and one daughter <u>nucleus</u> migrates into the bud.

* This fragment eventually detaches from the parent cell after the <u>nucleus</u> divides via <u>mitosis</u> and is capable of replicating using the same process.

* <u>Yeasts</u> (e.g., <u>Candida</u> spp.) mainly reproduce using this mechanism.

* Types of asexual spores

* Conidiospore: a single-cell, bicellular, or multicellular structure that arises on the tip or side of a hyphal structure called a “conidiophore” (e.g., <u>Aspergillus</u>)

* Sporangiospore: produced in a sac-like structure called sporangia (e.g., <u>Rhizopus</u>)

* Arthrospore: formed by the fragmentation of a disjunctor cell or splitting of a double septum (e.g., Trichosporidium, Coccididious immitis)

* Chlamydospore: a thick-walled, single-cell spore in or on <u>hyphae</u> (e.g., <u>Candida</u> spp.)

* Blastospore: a <u>budding</u> spore usually formed at the terminal end of a <u>hypha</u> (e.g., <u>Candida albicans</u>, Trichosporon spp., <u>Paracoccidioides</u> spp.)





#### Sexual reproduction of fungi




* Stages: plasmogamy, <u>karyogamy</u>, and <u>meiosis</u>

* Union of two <u>haploid</u> <u>hyphae</u> → fusion of the <u>cytoplasm</u>/protoplasm (plasmogamy) → fusion of the <u>nuclei</u> (<u>karyogamy</u>) → a <u>diploid</u> <u>zygote</u>

* Under appropriate environmental stimuli (e.g., light, temperature, <u>nutrients</u>), the <u>zygote</u> undergoes <u>meiosis</u> → production of sexual spores → germination

* Main methods of plasmogamy

* Gametangium

* An organ or cell in which <u>gametes</u> are produced

* The fusion of the entire contents of two contacting gametangia takes place via a pore-like structure or by direct fusion.

* Somatogamy: somatic <u>hyphae</u> take over the sexual function, come into contact, fuse, and exchange <u>nuclei</u>

* Spermatization: fungi male fungal structures called spermatia become attached to the female receptive <u>hyphae</u> or gametangia

* Types of sexual spores

* Ascospores: produced in a sac-like structure called an “ascus” (e.g., <u>Blastomyces</u>, <u>Histoplasma</u>, <u>Aspergillus</u>)

* Basidiospore: produced in a club-shaped structure called a “basidium” (e.g., <u>Cryptococcus</u>, Malassezia, Trichosporon)

* Zygospore: formed when two sexually compatible <u>hyphae</u> or gametangia fuse (e.g., <u>Rhizopus</u>)

* Oospores: a thick-walled spore, formed when a female <u>gamete</u> is fertilized by a male <u>gamete</u> <u>nucleus</u>. I.e., occurs solely in clinically nonrelevant fungi, e.g., Pythium, Phytophthora.





##### Sexual systems [[5]](/library/FJcgDW0)




* Overview

* There are two main modes of reproduction: <u>homothallism</u> and <u>heterothallism</u>

* Both modes share key reproductive features (e.g., <u>ploidy</u> changes, <u>meiosis</u>) but differ in features involving aspects of cell or hyphal fusion.

* Homothallism

* The possession of resources to reproduce sexually in a single fungus; i.e., the thallus contains both male and female sex organs, thus enabling self-<u>fertilization</u>

* Examples: <u>Aspergillus</u> nidulans, <u>P. jirovecii</u>

* Heterothallism

* The division of sexes between fungi of a single (self-sterile) species; reproduction occurs between two separate mycelia

* Example: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's <u>yeast</u>)





### Fungal metabolism [[1]](/library/bRYHlK)[[6]](/library/4Ic31d0)




#### Overview




* Fungi have a variety of metabolic pathways enabling them to digest and synthesize compounds.

* Fungi derive their energy from the breakdown of organic compounds.

* Organic compound breakdown is achieved via enzyme secretion (e.g., hydrolytic, oxidative, peroxidative)





#### Substances synthesized by fungi




* Primary metabolites

* Compounds responsible growth and <u>energy storage</u>

* Act as intermediates in the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites

* Examples: <u>pyruvate</u>, ethanol, <u>lactic acid</u>

* Secondary metabolites: compounds not essential to cellular life

* <u>Antibiotics</u>: e.g., <u>penicillins</u> by Penicillium chrysogenum, <u>cephalosporins</u> by Acremonium chrysogenum

* Toxins

* Aflatoxins by <u>molds</u> (e.g., <u>Aspergillus flavus</u>)

* Found on nuts, seeds, and grains

* Poisonous <u>carcinogen</u> associated with <u>hepatocellular carcinoma</u> (induces <u>TP53</u> mutation)

* Amanitins (see “<u>Amanita phalloides</u>”)

* <u>Ergot</u> alkaloids: ergotamine by <u>ergot</u> fungus (e.g., Claviceps purpurea)

* Found on grains, typically rye

* Causes <u>vasoconstriction</u> by binding to 5-HT1D <u>serotonin</u> <u>receptors</u> and <u>alpha-adrenergic receptors</u>

## Fungi overview

* <u>Dermatophytes</u>: filamentous fungi (mainly affect <u>skin</u> and <u>nails</u>)

* <u>Trichophyton</u>

* <u>Microsporum</u>

* <u>Epidermophyton</u> species

* <u>Yeasts</u>: <u>budding</u> fungi (may affect <u>skin</u>, <u>mucous membranes</u>, and internal organs)

* <u>Candida</u> species (particularly <u>Candida albicans</u>) cause <u>candidiasis</u>

* <u>Cryptococcus neoformans</u> causes <u>cryptococcosis</u>

* <u>Malassezia furfur</u> causes <u>pityriasis versicolor</u>

* <u>Molds</u>: <u>Aspergillus</u> fumigatus causes <u>aspergillosis</u> (may affect internal organs)

* <u>Dimorphic fungi</u>

* <u>Blastomyces dermatitidis</u>

* <u>Coccidioidomycosis</u> species

* <u>Histoplasma capsulatum</u>

* <u>Sporothrix schenckii</u>

* See “<u>Endemic fungal infections</u>.”

---

## Dermatophytes

* <u>Pathogenicity</u>

* <u>Dermatophytes</u> produce keratinase, which allows them to infect the <u>skin</u>, <u>hair</u>, and <u>nails</u>.

* Many <u>dermatophytes</u> are <u>obligate pathogens</u>.

* Morphology

* Form <u>hyphae</u> and <u>mycelium</u>

* After penetration into the <u>skin</u>, concentric propagation may occur around the entry site.

## Yeasts

* <u>Pathogenicity</u>

* Usually an <u>opportunistic pathogen</u>

* Can infect the <u>skin</u>, <u>mucous membranes</u>, or internal organs

* Morphology

* Demonstrate <u>budding</u> cells and <u>pseudomycelium</u>

* Single <u>yeast</u> cells are 5–8 μm in size.

* <u>Gram positive</u> staining





| Overview of the most important <u>yeasts</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Characteristics | Diseases | Treatment |
| Candida species | <br>* <u>Candida albicans</u> is the most common <u>Candida</u> species worldwide and is almost exclusively found in humans.<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vaginal yeast infection</u>, <u>balanitis</u><br><br>* <u>Erosio interdigitalis blastomycetica</u><br><br>* <u>Oral thrush</u><br><br>* <u>Candida esophagitis</u><br><br>* <u>Candidal intertrigo</u><br><br>* <u>Invasive candidiasis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Local: <u>ciclopirox</u>, <u>nystatin</u>, <u>clotrimazole</u>, <u>miconazole</u>, <u>ketoconazole</u><br><br>* Systemic<br><br>* IV <u>caspofungin</u> OR <u>micafungin</u> (<u>echinocandins</u>)<br><br>* Alternatively: <u>fluconazole</u>  OR <u>amphotericin B</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Cryptococcus neoformans</u> <br> | <br><br>* Humans are infected via contaminated dust particles.<br><br>* Possesses a capsule, which can be visualized using <u>India ink</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Cryptococcal meningitis</u><br><br>* <u>Cryptococcosis</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Amphotericin B</u> PLUS <u>flucytosine</u>, followed by <u>fluconazole</u> <u>maintenance therapy</u> for at least 12 months<br><br> |
| Malassezia furfur | <br><br>* Yellow-orange fluorescence under <u>Wood lamp</u><br><br>* Particularly present in the infundibulum of the <u>hair follicle</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pityriasis versicolor</u><br><br>* Involved in the pathogenesis of <u>seborrheic eczema</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Local: <u>selenium</u> sulfide lotion or shampoo, <u>miconazole</u>, <u>ketoconazole</u>, OR <u>terbinafine</u><br><br>* Systemic: <u>fluconazole</u> OR <u>itraconazole</u><br><br><br> |

## Molds

* <u>Pathogenicity</u>

* Usually an <u>opportunistic pathogen</u>

* <u>Mold</u> <u>antigens</u> are one of the most frequent causes of <u>allergies</u>.

* <u>Molds</u> produce various toxins. Infection is caused by either aerogenic uptake or is foodborne (e.g., <u>aflatoxins</u>).

* Morphology

* Formation of monomorphic septate <u>hyphae</u> that branch at 45° and <u>mycelium</u>

* <u>Mold</u> can infest food products and acquire a fuzzy appearance that is macroscopically visible.

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Aspergillus fumigatus</u> 

* Ubiquitous occurrence

* Some species produce <u>aflatoxins</u>

* Diseases

* <u>Aspergillosis</u>

* <u>Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis</u> (<u>ABPA</u>)

* <u>Aspergilloma</u>

* <u>Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis</u>

* <u>Endocarditis</u>

* Treatment

* <u>ABPA</u>

* Oral <u>prednisone</u> if severe

* <u>Itraconazole</u> if recurrent

* Pulmonary <u>aspergilloma</u>: <u>lobectomy</u>

* <u>Invasive aspergillosis</u>: IV <u>voriconazole</u>, <u>caspofungin</u>, amphotericin
